However, before dealing with the tax changes which I shall recommend, I would like to refer to our prospective cash position and those extra budgetary cash receipts and disbursements which are so important from the economic standpoint in their impact upon our economy and in appraising the real significance of our financial operations for the year.
To this prospective budgetary deficit of $375 million we must add our probable cash disbursements for other than budgetary expenditures. In the replacement fund set up under the Defence Appropriation Act there is a balance of $175 million which is now available to the Department of National Defence for cash expenditures for the purpose of replacing existing stocks of defence equipment transferred to our north Atlantic allies during the fiscal year just ended. During the new year additional transfers to our allies are expected, but substantial cash disbursements for replacements will also be made, and these disbursements are likely to exceed the transfers to the replacement fund, although the actual amount of the excess is difficult to forecast. In addition, we shall in all probability require about $60 million for housing loans, possibly $15 or $20 million for Veterans Land Act advances, and there will undoubtedly be other loans and investments. Offsetting these will be the cash receipts in the annuity and pension funds and in the various trust and other accounts, including repayments of loans and advances made in previous years. All in all, I expect that our total non-budgetary cash disbursements will somewhat exceed our total nonbudgetary cash receipts. This is apart from any transactions in our own securities, and possible advances to or repayments by the foreign exchange control board resulting from changes in the size of our exchange reserves. It is, of course, not possible to forecast with any degree of assurance the extent of any change in these exchange reserves and I shall not attempt that hazardous exercise. From what has been said, however, it seems apparent that unless the repayment of advances by the foreign exchange control board equals the net excess of non-budgetary cash disbursements over non-budgetary receipts, our over-all cash deficit, assuming no changes in our present tax structure, would exceed the estimate of our budgetary deficit I have already given,
The Budget-Mr. Abbott

I said a moment ago that we face a prospective deficit of $375 million. The first question is, what shall we do about it? In my mind, and I think in the mind of every hon. member, the answer is clear and must be unequivocal. No person with any sense of financial responsibility and having a clear view of our circumstances and our prospects could do other than conclude that we must increase our revenues by at least the amount of the deficit, that we must balance the budget, that we must follow a strict pay-as-we-go policy.
There is, of course, a certain arbitrary element about budget statistics. We do our budget arithmetic in terms of separate periods of time-the fiscal year. In reality the stream of income and the stream of expenditure are continuous though always changing. In some months the inflow exceeds the outflow, in others the process is reversed. Since the summer of 1950 the volume of flow in both streams has been steadily rising, though at varying rates. A year ago our total expenditures were $2-4 billion, in the year just closed they were $2 [DOT] 9 billion, this year they will be $3-7 billion. It will be clear that during the last few months of the past year the flow of expenditure was at a rate considerably above $2-9 billion a year, and during the last half of this fiscal year it will probably be running at a rate of about $3-9 billion a year.
It is my duty, therefore, to seek new revenues which will produce actual additional receipts of about $400 million in this fiscal year, but which will be yielding at a rate of about $600 million a year during the last six months of the year.
The next question is one of ways and means. It is generally agreed, I think, that we have an excellent basic tax structure. We arrived at this basic structure through a series of changes completed in 1948 and 1949. It consists of a well balanced blend of personal income taxes, corporation income taxes, succession duties and commodity taxes. The commodity taxes in turn comprise customs duties, the so-called general sales tax and the special excise taxes. This structure was designed to be simple and flexible, one that could be readily adapted by moderate changes in rates or in coverage to meet any reasonable scale of peacetime requirements.
I am reluctant to believe that we must inevitably face budgets of $4 billion or more for any considerable succession of years. There is still a possibility that reasonable solutions of the present international tensions may be developed. In another year's time we should have a clear view of the prospects. I have, therefore, decided not to recommend

The Budget-Mr. Abbott any major reconstruction of our tax system this year but instead to meet our current requirements by a series of simple but adequate surcharges on several existing taxes and also to widen the coverage of our special excise taxes. I think that over the shorter run this method of defence surcharges will produce the necessary revenue with the least difficulty and inconvenience. If our optimistic hopes are realized it will be easy to reduce these surcharges or to drop them entirely, but I want to add that if it becomes clear that we are in for a long pull at these high levels of expenditure some major changes in the existing tax structure may have to be devised. My tax proposals, therefore, must be regarded as an interim policy for the period of the current year.
In proposing tax changes in times like these we must give consideration to the effects of the inflationary forces at work. Our principal economic objectives at this time must be greater efficiency, greater output, less nonessential capital investment, moderation in consumer spending, and an increase in personal savings. At the same time we would all wish to retain as free and as flexible an economic system as possible. Taxes operate on the economic system by diverting part of the income stream and by altering price relationships, and they have the effect of varying the intensity of incentives to produce and to spend or save. Any tax change will have some effect on incentives, or on spending, or on saving. Our problem is to get a good balance between taxes on earnings and taxes on spending. Taxes on spending, that is, taxes on commodities, do not adversely affect incentives to produce. In the case of taxes on commodities, government revenue is obtained not by reducing private income, but by placing a surcharge on private expenditure of certain kinds. This type of taxation has the advantage that it does not adversely affect the incentive to earn income, that is, to produce, and it does offer the consumer some choice as to whether he will spend, and pay the tax, or whether he will save and to that extent avoid the tax.
As I said earlier, the three principal inflationary forces presently at work in Canada are the rising prices outside Canada, the domestic capital investment boom which shows no signs of abating, and the fact that consumer spending power is outrunning the flow and production of consumer goods and services. There is little we can do about rising external prices, but we can do a good deal about the two domestic pressures and we have already done a good deal.

Consumer expenditures are being restrained by consumer credit regulations, as well as by the higher taxes introduced last September, and will be further affected by the higher taxes I shall be proposing a little later this evening. Taken together we think that these measures are adequate to the circumstances.
Heavy capital expenditures, on the other hand, are providing the most severe internal pressure and all signs point to increasing pressure from this source. In 1950 they were much more than double 1946 and 50 per cent above 1947. The reported' capital expenditure plans for 1951 indicate intentions to increase them by a further 15 per cent over 1950, but it may be doubted whether such an increase is physically possible.
Capital expenditures are much more difficult to hold within bounds. Monetary and credit policies are having a restraining effect, but a large proportion of business corporations still have a highly liquid position and to that extent are less affected by these financial controls. The increases in corporation income taxes which I shall be proposing will drain off substantial amounts of corporate profits but the total volume of profits remaining in corporate hands will still be sufficient to maintain and, in some cases, to increase the capacity of corporations to plan additional capital investment without recourse to borrowed funds. Ordinarily this is a good thing both for the corporations and for the country, but under present conditions all expenditures of this sort that are not essential should be postponed.
Steel and related controls will place considerable restraints on less essential capital expansion, but they will not directly affect certain kinds of investment. In fact they could have the result of intensifying competition for such other materials and labour as are available. To embark upon all-out direct construction control would be an almost impossible task, as the experience of 1944-45 indicated.
What we need is a stiff financial deterrent that will affect particularly the businessman who is considering the kind of investment which is attractive, not because of its longterm soundness, but because it can be written off out of the expected high profits of the next few years at a time when he expects the rate of corporate income tax to be abnormally high.
To provide this deterrent it is proposed to defer for a period of four years the right to charge depreciation on all capital assets

acquired after April 10, 1951, excepting certain classes of assets defined in the regulations and certain additional kinds of assets when certified as eligible by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The principal classes of assets which will still be eligible for current depreciation without a certificate will be those acquired
(a)	for the production and distribution of electricity, gas and water; the provision of telegraph and telephone services; pipe lines, gas and oil well equipment; lumbering equipment; patents and franchises.
(b)	for use by individuals in farming, fishing, or a professional service.
The principal kinds of assets in respect of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be authorized, in his discretion, to issue certificates of eligibility for current depreciation will be those necessarily acquired for
(a)	defence purposes;
(b)	the production and distribution of primary products in the farming, fishing, mining, petroleum, lumber and pulp and paper industries;
(c)	direct use in a transportation or communication business.
Under the proposal, the right to charge depreciation as an expense is deferred, not cancelled or even diminished. For example, $10,000 of ineligible assets acquired after April 10, 1951, will earn no depreciation for tax purposes during the next four years; but in 1955 it can be transferred to the depreciable asset account at its full original cost. If it is a type of asset that can be written off in, say, 10 years, it will be written off in 1955-64 instead of in 1951-60.
The deterrent will particularly affect the businessman whose decision to make a capital expenditure is strongly* influenced by the expectation that he can write off a large fraction of his cost at a time when both profits and tax rates are abnormally high, particularly if it is a kind of investment with uncertain profit-making possibilities six or eight years hence. In other words it will compel the businessman to give primary attention to the long-term prospects of proposed capital expenditures and if outside financial participation is required lenders will also take this view.
There will, therefore, be a stiff deterrent on projects of uncertain long-run value and also on capital expenditures on frills, gadgets and generally "dressing up" offices, stores and buildings. This deterrent should reduce the competitive scramble for scarce materials
The Budget-Mr. Abbott and equipment and thus place less strain on direct controls. Such materials and equipment will tend to go to those who can make the best long-term use of them. Bidders who are anticipating short-run quick profits will tend to withdraw from the market. One further advantage is that the government will not be telling anyone that he cannot do this or that. What will happen is that a financial penalty will be put, in the short run, on those who go ahead with less essential expenditures.
These revised depreciation regulations will go into effect immediately and will apply to all capital assets acquired after April 10, 1951. A copy of the regulations which have been approved by the governor in council will be tabled at the close of my address and my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, will be issuing an explanatory statement within a day or two.
I turn now to my proposals for tax changes for this year.
The field of the corporation income tax is a difficult one, and one which I have to approach with a particularly keen sense of responsibility for the real national interest, because the general public does not, I am afraid, fully understand the implication of these taxes. It would be only too easy to take a superficially popular line and increase these taxes to a point which while yielding large immediate revenues would do grave damage in the longer run to the economy as a whole.
I shall not repeat what I said about the excess profits tax last September. I still believe that it is not a sound tax except under very special circumstances, and I do not believe we have reached that point. A part of what I said about the excess profits tax, namely, that it blunts the goad to efficiency and that it invites waste, applies also to high rates of corporation income tax. It is, of course, a question of degree. I say quite frankly, however, that I am not happy about corporation tax rates when they go over 50 per cent. I think it is bad psychology to permit people to say that more than half of any income earned, or any savings made, will go to the government.
There is also the point that corporation taxes involve double taxation; we tax the corporation on its profits, and then we tax the shareholder again on his dividends. Moreover, we have always relied on undistributed corporation profits to provide a large fraction of the capital required for expansion of our industries. At this juncture in our

The Budget-Mr. Abbott affairs, with heavy capital investment contributing to inflationary pressure, I shall not be too much concerned if higher tax rates leave less for reinvestment, but in the long run it is a good thing for the country that business should grow out of reinvested profits.
Having weighed all these factors I have come to the conclusion that the right policy at this time is to impose a defence surcharge of 20 per cent on all corporation income tax payments in respect of income earned after January 1, 1951, in addition to the 5 per cent higher tax rate imposed last September. This 20 per cent surcharge will apply only to profits now taxed at the 38 per cent rate. It will not apply to the rate of 15 per cent which applies to the first $10,000 of profits.
I am conscious of the fact, however, that this 20 per cent surcharge will weigh very heavily on those kinds of companies which for a variety of reasons, public control of rates or otherwise, are never able to earn more than a very modest rate on their capital. To such companies the next few years can offer little expectation of increased profits, yet many of them are engaged in activities which will require them to raise very large sums of additional capital for essential expansion. If we are not to cripple their borrowing capacity we must not cripple their capacity to earn their normal profits after tax. For these reasons I propose that the 20 per cent defence surcharge shall not operate so as to reduce the net income after federal tax, but before any provincial income taxes, of any company to a point below a 5 per cent return on capital employed.
Apart from this abatement the effect of the 20 per cent defence surcharge is to raise the rate of tax on all profits over $10,000 from 38 per cent to 45-6 per cent. It must be remembered that there are also provincial corporate income taxes.' In the eight provinces with tax rental agreements it is 5 per cent, and in Ontario and Quebec it is 7 per cent. This means that the marginal rate of combined tax will be just over 50 per cent in eight provinces, 52-6 per cent in Ontario and Quebec.
If this 20 per cent defence surcharge wrere applied to all profits its yield would be about $115 million in this fiscal year, and about $170 million in a full year. The abatement I have mentioned will cause some reduction in this yield. On the other hand, we shall pick up some additional current revenue incidental to the policy I have announced regarding deferred depreciation. What this amount will be cannot be more than an informed guess. I am inclined to the view that this increased
revenue will be rather more than the loss from the abatement of the surcharge and I have, therefore, put down $116 million this year and $175 million in a full year as my increased revenue from the corporation income tax.
There will in addition be a number of technical changes in the law covering corporation taxes, but none of these will have any significant economic or budgetary implications.
I turn now to the personal income tax. In line with my earlier statement that I wish to upset the present tax structure as little as possible this year, I am proposing to leave the exemptions and the percentage rate structure unchanged and rely upon a straight defence surcharge for the revenues we require. This surcharge will be 20 per cent on the amount of tax payable under the present rate structure and will take effect as from July 1, 1951. This means that the tax payable for the whole calendar year of 1951 will be increased by ten per cent, but commencing July 1 all payroll deductions will be one-fifth greater than in the present deduction tables and all other pay-as-you-earn instalments will be increased by one-fifth. I turn now to our third broad field of taxation, that of commodity taxes.

The Budget-Mr. Abbott
We propose to make no changes in the present scale of taxes on alcoholic beverages. Last September we increased these taxes by $22 million a year. The rates are now high, and I am aware that whenever we change these taxes we impose a good deal of inconvenience and some confusion upon the provincial authorities.
We propose, however, to increase the taxes on cigarettes and on manufactured tobacco. The cigarette tax is now $10 per thousand, and I am recommending an increase of $1.50 or a total of $11.50 per thousand, effective midnight tonight. This change will yield us $21 million this year and $26 million in a full year.
For some years now we have had a tax on cigarette papers and cigarette tubes which are used by those who "roll their own". This tax has become difficult to administer. I propose to repeal this tax and substitute for it a'higher tax on manufactured tobacco. To keep a reasonable proportion between the traditional relationship between the taxes on cigarettes and tobacco I am recommending an increase of 48 cents a pound on manufactured tobacco. A proportionate increase is also proposed with respect to the tax on raw leaf tobacco. I estimate that these changes will give us an additional $8 million this year and $9 million in a full year over and above the loss of revenue on cigarette papers and tubes.
Next I come to what we call the special excise tax, that is the tax now imposed at a rate of 15 per cent on such things as motorcars, radios, household electric appliances, cameras, jewelry, cosmetics and so on. We propose that this tax be increased to a rate of 25 per rent.
The house will also recall that last September we deliberately decided not to place this special tax on refrigerators, stoves and washing machines. I regret that we can no longer afford to leave these entirely free of extra tax, and I am recommending that a tax at 15 per cent be levied on all mechanically operated domestic refrigerators and washing machines and on all domestic cooking stoves except those designed to use coal or wood only.
In September a tax of 30 per cent was imposed on all candy, confectionery and chewing gum. Experience has shown that this rate has been too severe, and its effects upon the industry have been out of proportion in comparison with other taxed industries. We propose, therefore, to reduce this rate to 15 per cent.
These, like all other commodity tax changes, will be effective at midnight tonight.
As usual I must give public notice that no claims for refund arising out of tax reduc-

tions in respect of goods on which tax has been paid will be entertained by my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue.
I estimate the increase from 15 per cent to 25 per cent in existing taxes after taking account of the reduction in the tax on candy will yield an extra $44 million this year and $54 million in a full year. The new items to be taxed at 15 per cent should produce about $16 million this year and $21 million in a full year.
Finally I have given very careful thought to the so-called general sales tax. I say "so-called general sales tax" because it is really very far from being such. Our present sales tax has a very long list of exemptions. About ninety-five per cent of all foods are free of sales tax. All fuels and all building materials are exempt. I think it is safe to say that two-thirds of the average Canadian family's total spending is not touched by the sales tax. Contrary to the frequent assertion, the sales tax does not strike a higher proportion of the expenditures of the low income group. Calculations based on recent family budget studies made by the dominion bureau of statistics indicate that in the lowest income groups only about one-quarter of total income is spent on goods subject to sales tax; at the $3,000 a year level about one-third of the family income is spent on goods subject to this tax. This 33 per cent of income spent on taxed commodities extends to beyond the $6,000 a year level. Only when incomes exceed $7,000 or $8,000 a year does the proportion of income spent on goods subject to sales tax star! to decline, and this is just about the point where our income tax starts to become sharply progressive. To say that our sales tax is a harsh regressive tax simply is not true.
If hon. members have succeeded in following my estimates of additional tax yields they will realize that my proposals so fai leave me about $100 million short of mj necessary objective of $400 million to balance this year's budget. My range of choice tc secure this remaining $100 million is reallj limited to more than doubling the increase ] have already proposed in the personal income tax, which could only be achieved by a sharj lowering of exemption levels, or an increase in the sales tax. I do not say that we have reached the practicable limits of the income tax. Of course we have not. The new rates we are proposing are much below the peal rates of 1943 and 1944. But experience has shown that you cannot increase income taxes by too much in any one year without creatinj serious embarrassment to large numbers o: people in all income groups, and withou' seriously affecting economic incentives.

I have therefore come to the conclusion that the sound thing to do from the economic point of view, and the fair thing at this time, is to increase the sales tax. I believe also that this is the choice that will be preferred by the great majority of our people. We are not recommending any change whatever in the coverage of the sales tax, but we are proposing that its rate be increased from 8 per cent to 10 per cent, effective immediately. I estimate that this will yield additional revenue of $105 million this year and $125 million in a full year.
Finally, I have certain tariff changes to propose. The tariff negotiations which have been taking place at Torquay during the past six months have just been concluded. The purpose of these negotiations was to extend the Geneva and Annecy agreements for another three-year period, to increase the scope of these agreements by including more countries and a wider range of commodities, and further, to arrange for additional reciprocal concessions on products previously negotiated. The Canadian delegation has concluded negotiations, providing for further reciprocal concessions, with sixteen countries including the United States. It has been arranged between the countries represented at Torquay that the details of the agreements resulting from the negotiations will be announced by the participating governments on May 9. Consequently I am not in a position to review the results at this time.
The budget resolutions relating to the customs tariff which I am tabling contain proposals to carry out certain recommendations of the tariff board and to provide for reductions in a number of duties which would lower costs of production in our great primary industries of agriculture, mining and fishing. Other changes proposed would achieve improvements in the wording and classification of several items so as to remove anomalies and to facilitate administration.
Two years ago I referred the plastics and synthetic resin items in the tariff to the tariff board for inquiry and report. These items were last examined by the board in 1937. In view of the rapid technical changes which have been taking place in this new and expanding industry, it is not surprising that the existing items in the tariff have become obsolete. Because of the highly technical factors involved and the complexity of the problem I felt it particularly desirable to have a thoroughgoing inquiry by the tariff board before recommending any action. The exhaustive examination which the board has undertaken is not yet completed, but the board is of the opinion that
The Budget-Mr. Abbott there are certain special and pressing difficulties which should be dealt with at this time. Consequently the board has submitted an interim report in which it recommends the insertion of certain items into the tariff prior to submission of its full conclusions covering the whole of the synthetic resins and plastics field. I have included these recommendations in the changes which I am proposing in the budget resolutions. The board's recommendations are designed to achieve up-to-date provisions respecting both classification and rates. The rates recommended involve some increases and some decreases in existing rates of duty. The reasons which led the board to recommend these readjustments are fully set out in its interim report which I am tabling with the budget resolutions.
The other tariff proposals include changes which would widen the application of certain items pertaining to farm - equipment. They would provide for the free entry of such things as grain or hay driers, individual sprinkler irrigation systems and several items of dairy equipment when for use on the farm. Most of these were recommended to the government in the brief submitted by the federation of agriculture. The free entry of these items would be of considerable assistance to our farmers and is in accord with the government's policy, stated by my predecessor, Eight Hon. J. L. Ilsley in his budget speech of 1944, regarding the free entry of farm implements and machinery.
In respect of the fishing industry two changes are proposed. One would permit the free entry of diesel engines for installation in boats usedi exclusively for commercial fishing operations and the other would widen the provision for free entry of nets and lines to include nets and lines made of any material. Both my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries, and I have received many representations that these changes would be of significant assistance to the fishing industry. In view of the heavy dependence of the industry upon export markets it is in the general interest to reduce, wherever practical, tariff barriers which add to costs.
The changes proposed in the customs tariff affecting equipment used in the mining industry would widen the existing provisions to permit the entry of unfinished parts of the equipment specified, at the same reduced rates as are now granted to the fully finished parts. In a number of cases the provisions would be extended to cover additional items of equipment used in mining operations.
An amendment is proposed to the tariff item dealing with settlers' effects. A number of countries from which we seek to obtain immigrants find it necessary, owing to the

The Budget-Mr. Abbott shortage of exchange, to apply restrictions on the transfer of emigrants' capital. These restrictions have operated as a deterrent to the movement of desirable immigrants into Canada. The new subsection which I am proposing to add would, in these cases, permit the free entry of settlers' effects during a period of three years from the time of the settler's first arrival. This would enable the settler to use his frozen capital to purchase and bring in from his country of origin such things as household effects, wearing apparel, tools of trade and agricultural equipment, after the settler has been here and has had1 an opportunity to decide what he and his family need most urgently. This new provision should make it possible for many desirable immigrants to establish themselves more rapidly in productive activity in this country.
Finally, I am proposing an amendment to tariff item 708. This would remove obsolete language and would enable the government to carry out reciprocal' customs arrangements regarding certain matters with other signatories of the North Atlantic treaty. These would apply to supplies for defence establishments located in one another's territory in accordance with jointly agreed plans for our common defence.
The net effect of all these tariff changes on the total of all customs revenues will not be significant.

Mr. Speaker, the minister must be pleased and perhaps a trifle surprised to And how popular his new taxes are; and perhaps it is just as well that he did not get the applause before he made his speech or he might have made them even higher. Whatever our differences with the minister are, I am sure I can say that we all recognize the heavy burden which he carries and that we appreciate the manner in which he discharges his heavy duties.
I do not propose tonight to enter into the details of the taxes which the minister has propounded. These can be gone into as we continue this debate. There are not many surprises, after all. The known taxes are there, and there are not many places for him to go when he wants substantial amounts of money.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, when the minister was speaking of millions and tens of millions of dollars, I was thinking most of the time of the people to whom millions and tens of millions are rather meaningless and whose financial calculations are limited to figuring whether or not they are going to be able to get by this week with prices as they stand now. We know how many of these people there are among us; and not all the glowing figures we have, showing the wonderful progress that we have made, alter the fact
that we have among us tens of thousands of people to whom these figures mean nothing. Indeed, it is a bitter irony that we are not able to manage our affairs well enough so that these people can be relieved of the necessitous situation in which they find themselves.
Having said this, I would say to the minister that it is a great disappointment to find that there is no indication tonight-none so far as I can see-that the minister is prepared to consider further measures to deal with this situation. Notwithstanding the fact that apparently we are the only civilized country, if we can call it that, which is not trying to deal with this matter, he goes cm persisting in a blank negation. I confess that after what the minister told us the other day I had hoped-although he did not, I must admit, put it in so many words-that we should have something different from this1 blank negation.
But I must admit the minister was surprisingly optimistic. He found a satisfaction which I am not able to share in various aspects of what he had to bring forward. He compared us with other countries and admonished us that we should be extremely thankful to be as well off as we are. My answer to that is this. What other country has the natural advantages that we have? What
1826	HOUSE OF

Then the minister went on to tell us as to what the government had done. First of all, they balanced the budget. I appreciate the balancing of the budget; but of course when the minister takes nearly $4 billion of our money, it is quite easy to balance the budget. I suppose if he had taken $500 million more, we would have had a $500 million larger surplus. When the minister takes satisfaction out of the great buoyancy of revenue, I must say that to me there is a certain amount of irony in that. I do not think he gave us the figures to show how much of that buoyancy was caused wholly by high prices. I think he mentioned high prices-

It would be a very substantial amount indeed, and there is precious little happiness to be got out of that realization. The minister told us about the economies, and all I wish to do on that score is to read a short extract from the Winnipeg Free Press which, I understand, is not usually regarded as particularly hostile to the government.
Just certain sections of it.

What the Winnipeg Free Press of March 16 last said is this:
The federal government's estimate of expenditure in the next fiscal year shows clearly that economy as a weapon against inflation has failed. The government has sharply reduced its expenditures in various departments, but these savings are almost entirely counterbalanced by increases elsewhere.
Then they mention the $35 million and say that in a non-defence budget of $1,922 million that is not big enough to be any good.
Then the minister mentioned consumer credit, and I will deal with that subject briefly. We passed legislation here last September. Having tried our best to create the impression in the minds of the government that there was a real emergency, we passed legislation with regard to consumer credit. The minister tells us, and correctly, that certain restrictive measures were put into effect in November and that more restrictive measures were put into effect in March of this year. But those put into effect last November were just a token. You might as well have waved a wand, for all the effect they had. I will say that those in March were better. But up to the present-and I wish to make this point, Mr. Speaker-none of these measures has had really any substantial effect at all.


Then we come to what the minister calls exercising influence on credit. Actually, I would remind the minister that the Bank of Canada was established for the purpose of regulating credit and currency, and I do not think anyone who knows the relationship between the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks doubts for one moment that when the Bank of Canada speaks the chartered banks listen.
Now, what is the situation with regard to our monetary policy? In a word, Mr. Speaker, I would remind you that for years, and in spite of all that could be said from this side of the house, we have had what is called an easy money policy. It was devised in 1945 when depression was expected, and it was used all through the successive years in spite of the fact that we were in a boom. The Winnipeg Free Press, if I may quote that friendly organ again, calls it the big blunder. Last September we urged-and the minister seemed to indicate he was going to take it seriously-that there should be a real attempt to curb credit. What was the result? What happened after that? During the autumn months, from September to November, there were $400 million of new bank loans. Approximately we created $400 million in addition to what there had been before. In other words, Mr. Speaker, this new money comes into competition with the wages, salaries and other earnings of the people of Canada and helps to sky-high the prices.
Order.
Get those high cost of living people out of the back.

I want to
ask this question, Mr. Speaker. What hope have we had held out tonight? My answer is that so far as dealing with these high prices is concerned we have had nothing but a blank negation. I repeat what I said a moment ago. Apparently we are alone in this. All other nations are prepared to act, and we are not prepared to act. We have to wait and see. We have to hope that something will turn up.
Let me make clear, Mr. Speaker, that I am not asking for rabbits out of a hat, I am not asking for a rigid system of over-all controls. What I am asking for is something flexible, something sensible. I want to say that the most responsible and reputable authorities do agree that in these emergent days emergent measures may be taken. I refer to such well known organs as the London Economist and to a well known American economist called Slichter, and to a very responsible and conservative organ

produced each month by the National City Bank. All of these speak of measures which may be taken temporarily and in an emergency, such as most of us in this house, most of us at any rate in this party, believe in, and I think if they could vote freely most of the people in this house have the same feeling.
In conclusion I wish, so far as my voice can carry, to let the people of Canada know that this emergency has been created in substantial measure by government neglects and defaults. I repudiate entirely the idea that this has just happened, that it is just a phenomenon, to use the word that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) used the other day, a sort of act of God; that we have nothing to do with it. I repudiate that entirely. But I go on to say that in spite of these mistakes and neglects the government have the temerity to return a virtual negative to everything that we can ask.
The government is always telling us of their great majority, but I would venture to ask them: In the light of what is happening now, how long do they think they can turn their backs on the people and still say that they have the people at their backs?
On motion of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) the debate was adjourned.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

I have no desire to detain the house very long this evening after the very masterly budget that we have heard presented by the Minister of Finance. However, I do want to deal very briefly with two or three points which have arisen, or which have presented themselves to my mind during this debate on the amendment of the leader of the opposition.
The question that is raised by this amendment, Mr. Speaker, is a very difficult one to deal with briefly, and I will not presume even to attempt to deal with it, but I have one or two observations that I feel should be made.
I think this debate exemplifies something that the Minister of Finance said in delivering his budget, namely, that there are no great divisions of fundamental policy in Canada on questions of this kind. I think it is clear that we are all agreed on the
Cost of Living
seriousness of the threat of inflation, and the necessity of having taken effective action to meet it.
The differences between us, Mr. Speaker, are purely on the details of how this problem should be met and what action should be taken to meet the rising cost of living, which is one of the symptoms of inflation. It has been said by a number of speakers that the people of Canada are disturbed by the effect upon their living of the rising cost of almost everything that Canadians have to buy. I think it is true. I know it is true that the Canadian people are disturbed about this and other effects of inflation.
While I was home during the Easter recess I discussed this problem with a number of people. In one particular instance, representatives of the railway brotherhood waited upon me to express to me the views of their membership. They expressed to me their belief that the government should institute price and rental control, and they asked me to place their views on this question before parliament, which I am doing this evening. I found myself unable to agree with the opinion expressed by that delegation, and I tried as best I could to explain to them the reason for which I held somewhat different views, and the reasons why I had a different idea of the proper approach to this problem.
Many of these reasons have been dealt with in the speeches of members who have preceded me in this debate. I do not propose to go over the ground that has already been thoroughly covered. I should like to state briefly some of the reasons why I believe that the decisions taken so far by the government on these questions have been a correct policy for this country to follow.
First, in my view price or rental controls are only one part of the attack on inflation, and they are a part of that attack which cannot stand alone. Our friends in the C.C.F. used to tell us a great deal about the controls and the wonderful experiences they were having in England with the maintenance of controls. We do not hear so much about the English experience these days. This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) questioned a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that at the present time the inflationary trends in Great Britain were stronger than they were in Canada. Perhaps a year or so ago the hon. member would have questioned that statement most violently, but today he contented himself with questioning its absolute accuracy and tried to leave the impression that the Minister of Trade and

Cost of Living
Commerce had1 somewhat exaggerated the inflation being experienced in England.
However that may be, I think the English experience not only proves that price control alone will not contain inflation but it proves that a rigid over-all system of controls on prices, on rents, on wages, on manpower and the whole panoply of direct controls cannot indefinitely answer this problem. While under this system the English people for the past few years have been protected to some extent from paying the price of inflation through a rising cost of living, all that time they have been paying that price through the creeping paralysis of austerity and now a situation has developed where even these controls will not keep the cost of living down and in addition they are going to have to pay the price in a rising cost of living.

May I ask
the hon. member the same question he asked the hon. member for Vancouver East? The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the cost of retail prices had gone up 15 per cent in Canada and about 21 or 23 per cent in the United Kingdom, but that the cost of living index had not gone up very much in the United Kingdom.
It costs more to live over there than it does here.

You do not
know what you are talking about.
Certainly I do.

The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) has a strange idea of what is a question, but that is exactly the point I raised with the hon. member for Vancouver East. The point is that if the over-all index of retail prices as opposed to the cost of living has gone up 23 per cent in Great Britain it is simply because the rises so far have been in items that are not heavily weighted in the cost of living index. When these rises in prices become effective in items that are heavily weighted in the cost of living index then the inflationary pressures which are at work will become apparent in the index. The only thing that differentiates the British situation from ours is the fact that these effects have not become apparent in the cost of living index, but they will.
The headline in the Ottawa Journal today reads:
Britons get "Black Budget"
Hardly a person escapes tougher austerity orders.
That indicates the situation which the British public unfortunately faces at the present time. They have been paying the 
price of inflation in austerity and are now beginning to pay it as well in a rising cost of living.
The second point I should like to outline briefly is the obvious inability of Canada or any other country to deal with extraordinary advances in the cost of basic imports coming from other countries. This is an element in the cost of living which we cannot possibly control with price or any other control within the country.
Third, I do not believe that the Canadian people should be called upon to accept or are ready to accept over-all controls that would be required if we are to embark immediately upon a system of price and other controls. With price control we would have to foresee the inevitability, either immediately or within a short time, of wage and salary controls. With wage and salary controls being applied we would have to foresee almost immediately some form of selective service. When we get to that stage, or perhaps even before, we would have to foresee some form of widespread allocation of materials and the imposition of severe export controls as well. In the background of the whole picture is the question of substantial subsidies, either at the manufacturing or at the consumer level.
I think that anyone in this house who advocates the imposition of price or any other control of a general nature must be prepared to take the responsibility of stating that he believes that we should consider an economic procedure of taking gradually, or perhaps in a short space of time, all these controls into the Canadian economy. I was struck by one paragraph in the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), who moved this amendment the other day. At page 1736 of Hansard of April 9 he is reported as saying:
The government has contended that no nation in the world did a better job of price and other controls than Canada did during the last war.
I do not think the hon. gentleman will find anyone who will dispute the truth of that statement. He then went on to say:
In that effort they were assisted by very able economists. The experience of those men and women is available today. The government can take advantage of that experience and with the knowledge they possess, knowledge we do not possess as to what controls they are going to impose on production and supply, they can design price and other controls appropriate to meet the situation which will result from their action at the production and supply level.
I presume that those are the same gentlemen who were characterized a year or eighteen months ago as being Marxists and dangerous to the Canadian nation. The fact is, as was pointed out last evening by the

Minister of Trade and Commerce, the government is doing exactly what the leader of the opposition urged them to do in the paragraph I have quoted. The experience is that all these gentlemen who are referred to as having assisted and advised the government in the operation of the control procedures of the last war are advising the government unanimously that in the present circumstances such controls simply will not work. On that basis I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government is taking very good advice from these gentlemen, and is doing exactly what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has suggested that they should do.
I should simply like to say that I regard the amendment as an invitation to the house to register a false decision that we do not have confidence in the present government, and the basis for that false decision would be that our lack of confidence arises out of the government's refusal to embark on the kind of direct controls being advocated by the hon. gentleman opposite. My opinion is that the government is being well advised, is being wise, and, because of the anti-inflationary policies which it is following and will continue to follow, far from deserving a vote from us expressing lack of confidence it deserves our faith, wholehearted confidence and support.

Mr. Speaker, in the last paragraph of his speech the last speaker actually said all that I intended to say tonight. I really wanted to explain why I could not possibly vote for the amendment. In the first place it is a motion of lack of confidence. Is there anyone else in this house in whom anybody could hope to have confidence to replace the government now in authority? Naturally I have to vote against the amendment. Personally I think that controls are inevitable sooner or later but I do not want controls that, when put into effect, will start at the level of the farmers as they did last time. I think the finest education for anyone who is going to institute controls, or who is going to have anything to do with their operation, would be to spend a month on a dairy farm as an active worker, not merely as an onlooker like so many of those in high places who tell us that they were brought up on a dairy farm and took good care to get out when they were young.
A neighbour of mine with a very important position has a nineteen year old son who worked in the lumber business for six months and then was promoted. He gets $15 a day. Of course I am speaking of the province of British Columbia where we pay proper wages, not some of the more backward 50709-117
Cost of Living
provinces. This boy receives $15 a day for an eight hour day. His father, who holds a very responsible position corresponding almost to that of a deputy minister at Ottawa, gets $250 a month, and no travelling expenses. His uncle across the road, with a $25,000 investment, milks cows 365 days a year and makes $12 a day. That is one reason why I do not think we are ready for controls yet. I am too much afraid that they will be put on at the farmers level.
There can be no question that the cost of living has gone up. We had an example of it tonight. I was more fortunate than some, as you can see. I borrowed $10 from the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and bought every cigarette I could possibly lay my hands on, after the new tax was announced. I had no compunction in doing that. I am not a hoarder but I did that tonight. I want to express the opinion that I think it is utter-I cannot use the language I should like to, and I am not ashamed to say that I have used a little of it in my time-nonsense not to tax alcohol and to tax cigarettes. I do not think that meets with the approval of even ten per cent of the people of Canada. I will have more to say about that at the right time and will make many forty-minute speeches when the resolutions are before the house. That is one thing that I should like to impress on the government to the best of my ability.
As I said, I will certainly vote against the amendment because it is a straight vote of confidence in the government, and I have every confidence that the government will work out a solution. I think they are a bit backward so far as the people I particularly want to deal with tonight are concerned, the burnt-out veterans and those on soldiers pensions. I do not know just how it is possible to expedite the matter but I would suggest a bonus. It has been pointed out to me that we are providing a 20 per cent pay increase for judges. I listened the other night to a discussion about a subsidy to take useless gold out of the ground. I have not heard anything about a subsidy for the man who is milking cows 365 days of the year. I have a local paper here that concerns the people of my community, and there is a headline reading, "Low Bond Quote Jeopardizes District School Building Plans." The school bonds had to be sold at 92-75, and it is one of the wealthiest municipalities in the province of British Columbia. The municipality of Burnaby-I venture this statement-is one of the largest in population and assessment in the Dominion of Canada, and they could not get an offer on their school bonds at all. That is a pretty serious state of affairs.

Cost of Living
I want to emphasize that if controls are instituted-and personally I think that eventually they will be in some form or other-they must not be put into effect at the producers level. We hear all sorts of talk about milk when it goes up a cent. I did not hear anybody in the house, and very few outside, complain when beer went up four cents, or whatever it did go up, but as soon as milk goes up we hear about it. I have heard members of the house with incomes of over $25,000 a year complaining about the price of butter, but they would not know which end or which side of a cow to start milking, let alone do it for 365 days in a year.
Which side is it?

I can tell you because
I am a practical farmer and not a graduate of a university of agriculture. That will hold you.
Not for long.

We have set up a
veterans affairs committee, and I understand that I am a member of it. I hope that the first thing they will take up will be the question of finding some means or other of urging upon the government the plight of these veterans. I know that every member of the government and of the house, including the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), is just as sympathetic to the veterans as I am. I think every member wants to see that no one suffers but anyone who has travelled around Canada at ail-I was going to use the words "lower level" but that is not correct-and visited the ordinary rank and file in the dominion knows that there is suffering at the present time. He must know and appreciate that there is tremendous suffering amongst those on fixed incomes, particularly those on old age pensions, veterans pensions or any other kind of pension.
Naturally I am particularly interested in veterans pensions because I am closely associated with the veterans. There are veterans widows suffering from arthritis who are receiving the magnificent sum of $40 a month on which they are expected to live. As I see it, that is not good enough. I do not care what steps the government takes to bring justice to these people. That is a matter for some of the experts and economic authorities who abound in Ottawa. The only things we have more of in Ottawa than economic authorities are the lobbyists at the Chateau Laurier. I hope the government will take steps very soon so far as those on pensions and other fixed incomes are concerned. I should like to urge upon the
	-
government strongly that, if and when controls are instituted, they should not be based on the producer level entirely as they were the last time, remembering at all times that the farmer is not only a producer but a consumer as well.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from a part of the country which feels the effects of rising prices more than any other, where we rely on imports for such a large proportion of our food and clothing, I feel that I must take part in this debate and support the amendment which has been proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I believe that amendment is supported also by the great majority of the people of this country today.
What we have heard from the members and supporters of the government are technical objections rather than arguments in principle against the imposition of controls to prevent prices rising. I do not believe any question is agitating the minds of the people of this country at the present time so much as the rise in the cost of living. Other hon. members have referred to various groups who are affected. Let us begin with the civil servants, the people working for the government, the very people upon whom they depend to carry out this magnificent program we have heard about. What do they think about the cost of living? Here is an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 5 under the heading, "Civil service asks further raise or living cost bonus. Swiftly rising tide of prices alarms government staff". It says:
Mr. Whitehouse stressed that the main reason for the soaring of the index was due to marked increases in the price of food. The public service had recently received a salary revision but the increases are still 10 per cent behind living costs. The increases covered costs as of last September, he said. There are indications they are not going to stop unless controls are clamped on immediately.
That is the view of the people working for the government, a large class of people in this country. I do not knew whom the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) was referring to when he said the government was depending upon the experts who carried out the price control policy during the last war. That must be a very select few at the top, not the great majority of civil servants.
Then take the next class of people who have been referred to, the civil service pensioners. How do they feel about the effect of rising costs of living? Only the other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) told the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that he was tired answering this point. He did not bother going into details at the time, but he told me afterwards that the civil servant buys his pension, and if he

does not buy enough pension that is his own lookout and nothing can be done for him. When the cost of living goes up 15 or 16 points in a year the civil service pensioner who gets $50 or $100 a month finds that the value of his pension has decreased appreciably, and he and his wife are under stress and anxiety while the government appears to be cynical about it.
Take another group of persons, the old age pensioners, who prior to the election of 1949 were promised $40 a month. How much has the cost of living gone up since 1949, and how much is that $40 worth today? The cost of food, which is a major item, was estimated at 203 in 1949. It is now estimated at 220, an increase of 17 points. The cost of living in 1949 was 160. Now it is almost 180, an increase of 20 points. In other words money has depreciated by 14 per cent in that time. A great many persons who have become entitled to pensions within the last five or ten years are terribly affected by the rise in the cost of living since 1945, when we began to remove the controls. There are also the veterans and people living on fixed incomes, such as widows and orphans, and people who get their income from government bonds. All these people are affected; so are the workers and the farmers. Only today we had a delegation here interviewing the government asking that price controls be put on. I think I can speak for the fishermen who had to take at least 50 per cent less for their catch last fall. How can anyone expect them to make a living with rising costs? It would also be interesting to point out that the value of the indemnity paid members of parliament has declined by about 12 per cent. We would need $4,750 to equal what the member of parliament received two years ago. But the judges are being given special consideration.

speechtext: Are you in favour of an increase in the indemnity?

I am sure the minister has much more influence than I have and he should see that justice is done. I see it is going to be done to the judges. There is a resolution on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Justice to increase the salaries of judges, to increase the number of judges and to provide certain adjustments as to the pensions of judges and widows of judges. I wonder if that is to make allowance for the increase in the cost of living. If it is, we shall hear more about it when that matter is debated, because they are not the only people affected, and they are better able to bear it than the classes I have referred to.
This attitude on the part of the government reminds me of the attitude of the commission 80709-1174
Cost of Living
government in Newfoundland during the war. As president of the civil service association I had occasion to head many a delegation to interview that government asking for either price controls or a cost of living bonus for the civil service. On each occasion we were told, "Oh, it is impossible for us to put on controls. We have to import so much of our goods; we depend on outside sources, and we cannot do anything about it." But what happened? After the cost of living had gone up about 60 points they put on controls, and then they started talking about a cost of living bonus. It seems to me that is what this government is doing now. It is ashamed to admit that it is last in the field, that the opposition has brought up this matter which is so vital to the great majority of the people of this country. The government do not want to admit they have been wrong.
I can appreciate that there are certain difficulties about introducing controls, and that the government is reluctant to set up elaborate machinery such as we had during the last war. Despite the success of the control policy and the reputation the Canadian government gained through its operation from 1941 to 1945, last evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said he had not met anyone who had administrative experience in controls during the last war who was in favour of putting on the same type of controls again. Everyone who speaks of this talks about the same type of controls, and no one explains what he means by it. We have to control prices; the people who have had experience with rising prices are very anxious to see them stop soaring, and we have all met people like that. The government is well aware of the inflation that exists at the present time. During the past day or so the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) wrote a letter to the Ottawa branch of the Canadian consumers' association, which appeared in the Citizen of this morning. In it he said:
As you are aware, the government has attempted to mitigate inflationary pressures by attacking the problem at its roots.
Today we heard a very interesting lecture by one Hans Selye, a Czech doctor, who told us there were two kinds of treatment practised by doctors. One was the causative treatment, getting at the roots and eradicating the disease, like cutting out a cancer. The other one was the symptomatic treatment to relieve the symptoms. The symptom we want relieved at the present time is the increase in prices. The government does not have to solve all the economic problems, but can stop the rise in the price of necessities which the people of this country are

Cost of Living
facing today. The public is clamouring for these controls. What if the public is right and the government is wrong? What if the opposition is right and the government is wrong?
There are certain people, sir, who are protected by the fact that in making agreements they have taken the precaution of having an escalator clause inserted, which is attached to the cost of living index. From the Ottawa Journal I have an item which states that the people working for the municipality of Ottawa will get a monthly cost of living bonus of about $10,000, because in the agreement they made with the city of Ottawa there was a provision that when the cost of living went up they were to be recompensed. The 1,400 employees will be paid, but the Ottawa firemen who recently signed a similar cost of living bonus agreement will not benefit from the most recent jump in the index. The firemen's bonus does not become effective until the April cost of living figure. The Ottawa municipal service association members will be paid 35 cents per head per week for every point increase in the index since June, 1950. That amounts to about 13 points, and multiplied by 35 cents it equals $4.50 per week for each one of those 1,400 employees. The article reads:
Finance commissioner Gordon told city council at the last meeting the city would have to pay bonuses amounting to $260,000 on point increases to the end of January, 1951.
It can be seen from that there are certain people who will not be affected to the same extent as those who have no protection. The government seems to be indifferent to those who have no protection.
Tonight, sir, we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) deliver his budget. Anyone who heard him must be filled with admiration for this remarkable country that has such enormous wealth, and has such a capacity to meet tremendous expenditures of the kind indicated here this evening; a budget of nearly $4 billion expenditure can be met by the imposition of an extra billion dollars in taxes during the coming year. I think it is a marvellous feat for the Minister of Finance to attempt, but for him to say at the same time that this will not result in an increase in the cost of living is palpably absurd. Those people who are going to have increased corporation taxes are going to raise their profits. It has been stated here that the profits of companies during the past year have risen. Mr. Speaker, in my opinion they have risen out of all bounds.
Anyone who looks at the Financial Times report on companies operating in this country, a special edition of which was issued a short time ago, will see that the value of
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West) .1
stocks went up and profits went up. Some of the companies made very many millions in profits, and had hundreds of millions of dollars increase in the valuation of their shares during the past year. Is the government indifferent to the remarkable amount of money that these companies have made during the past year? From the statement of the Minister of Finance it seems that they are indifferent. Certainly, they are more friendly disposed towards corporations than they are towards that class of person who is dependent upon government action to help him achieve a decent standard of living. I cannot see anything in the budget that is going to reduce the cost of living. I cannot see anything in it except what will increase the cost of living. The minister mentioned a few things he was doing, but most of them are already in effect and they are not doing what he expected they would do. Last September he introduced measures that he thought were going to put down inflation. A month ago he introduced a measure to control credit. These measures have produced no results up to now, and I doubt very much whether they are going to show any results. I do not see anything that he has mentioned here tonight that is going to reduce the cost of living. The things in which the majority of the people in this country are interested are food, clothing and rent. I see nothing in the budget that is going to bring down the cost of those items.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) recommended that we avoid panic buying. I cannot imagine that the old age pensioners or the veterans or the civil servants -I do not know what they are like in this part of the continent but I know that in Newfoundland most of them were in debt nearly all their lives because salaries could never catch up with the cost of living-are going to engage in panic buying. There may be certain classes of people who will do so. Anyone who analyses the income tax reports will see that it is a comparatively small proportion of the population who have incomes of over $5,000 a year, and that is the class to whom the minister was referring.
We know that one of the causes of the increased cost of living is the decline in farm production. People are leaving the farms and going to the factories. I do not know what the government can do to encourage people to work on farms, but there is no doubt that we need to have more food produced if we want to have a sounder economy. It seems to me that the government is altogether too complacent about this situation. They are talking in a technical language which is over the heads of the people. The people cannot

understand what they are talking about. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), generally so genial, seems to be unperturbed about this situation.
There are two kinds of inflation. There is the open inflation that we are watching, and there is inflation that might take place if you have controls such as they now have in the United States. Mr. Donald Gordon, who was the head of the price control system during the war, says it is better to have control than inflation. I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is better. I cannot understand the hesitancy of the government, in the face of the critical conditions under which a large proportion of the people are living. Why are they so indifferent? I appeal to them not to be worried about losing face because they have to accept an amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). Let the government remember that the amendment is supported by the majority of the people of this country. If we had a secret ballot in this chamber tonight, I believe that the majority of the hon. members supporting the government would vote in favour of that amendment because they know that every class of person, farmer, fisherman and workers of all kinds, is in favour of controls to curb the rising cost of living.

Cost of Living
who have been good citizens of Canada for from ten to thirty years; and only by their having served in the imperial forces during the war do they differ from any other Canadians. They have contributed as much as any other Canadian to build up this country in those ten to thirty years. If, as has been indicated1 so far, government action is not to take place beyond what has been suggested by the budget to curb the rising cost of living, which curbing would give these men a reasonable hope that the worst is over, that hope has been denied them tonight.
I suggest that, failing direct action of price control, the government should seriously consider making up to these men the difference between the pound and the dollar, by fixing a higher rate of exchange for the pound paid in the form of imperial pensions. I do not mean to have that procedure apply to every small pension that is paid but rather to those who are in receipt of, I would suggest, a pension of 60 per cent to 100 per cent or are totally disabled. Many of these people could qualify for the old age pension, but the government does not have to pay it because they are getting a British pension. They could quite easily qualify for the old age pension in Canada if they did not receive this pension. I therefore do not see that the government would lose a great deal by subsidizing them or making up the difference in exchange in order to give these people a self-supporting pension that would keep them off public relief or from applying for the old age pension.
The same pressing argument could be advanced for all pensioners in the lower bracket of pensions, such as the blind and the old age pensioners and that vast number of men and women who are classified as incurable, whose total income depends on the generosity of friends or relatives. I do not need to enlarge upon the pitiful plight of these people. Hon. members are all aware of it and of the conditions under which the old people live, and how they try to maintain even a semblance of a standard of living, naturally receiving a periodical shock that we all receive when the cost of living spirals up a few more points. Even before the bureau of statistics informs us of this spiralling increase, these old people are fully conscious of it. They have already been to their grocer or to their butcher and have found that prices have gone up and that they have had to pay that much more for their needs. It does not take an index to bring home to any individual, particularly those in the lower brackets, the fact that the cost of living has

gone up. If for no other reason than to protect the living standards of these people whom I have mentioned, I think the government should take immediate action to prevent any further rise in the cost of living and that it should lay plans for a roll-back of prices.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) has on the order paper a resolution, and I hope it comes before the house, asking for an increase in the allowable income of old age pensioners. In case an opportunity is not given to bring it before the house I would certainly make that plea now on behalf of old age pensioners. If the cost of living is not to be curbed at the present level, at least grant to them an allowable income at an increased rate.
There is one other group to which I would like to refer, one in my own particular riding, namely the workers in the fruit industry. The main industry of our valley is fruit production, packing, shipping and so on. Naturally, by the very nature of the industry, we have a great number of parttime workers whose total income for the year is not high, although their income for one month, two months or three months while they are working may be quite decent. These people have given a great deal of thought to the spiralling cost of living. I should like to read part of a letter which I received from the Okanagan district trades and labour council early this year. It reads in part as follows:
Dear Sir:
The continuing upward spiral in the cost of living, which is the cause of considerable and growing apprehension among all Canadians, was the subject of close study at the last regular monthly meeting of the Okanagan district trades and labor council, held in Kelowna on Sunday, January 7 last.
As a result of the discussion, I was instructed to write to you, in your capacity as member of parliament for the Yale constituency, requesting your support in the next session of parliament for the enactment of price control legislation as outlined in the joint statement issued under recent date by the four major trade union centres, a copy of which I enclose for your information.
In order that there may be no mistake as to the attitude of the trade unions on this matter, and particularly the trade union that took the trouble to write to me, which is a very flourishing union operating largely in the Okanagan, I would like to read what they refer to as the views expressed by the four major unions of Canada. I am quoting from their brief in part:
The four trade union centres at the end of the war urged that price controls be maintained and at no time since have we retired from that position. We have always been unanimous in saying that the immediate result of the removal of controls would be the sky-rocketing of prices making it more difficult for average Canadian families to meet

their household requirements and maintain themselves in decency and dignity. We were repeatedly told by spokesmen for the government, however, that once price controls were removed prices would level off and automatically adjust themselves.
Our warnings went unheeded. The ill-timed removal of price controls led to an alarming increase in the price of all commodities, an increase which is still continuing. The effectiveness of control measures is well illustrated by the government's own figures. During the war under controls the cost of living index rose only 5.0 points between December, 1941, and April, 1946. Since April, 1946, when controls were removed, the cost of living index has shot up 50 points from 120.8 to 170.7 on November 1, 1950.
Statements to the effect that wage increases are the cause of higher prices are misleading. Since the removal of controls, prices have been free to rise at the will of the employer. Wages, on the other hand, can only be adjusted by negotiation, conciliation or even arbitration.
In connection with the wages of this particular group, they have an escalator clause, which works in a different way from the ordinary escalator clause. It is closely tied in with fruit prices. If the fruit prices go up the wages go up. If the fruit prices go down, the wages go down. In that way the worker in this industry has played his part in trying to keep prices down.
Finally, I would appeal particularly on behalf of the imperial veterans, that the government give serious consideration to the fact that these people are doubly penalized, first, by having to accept a drop of from $3.80 to $2.90 in the pound, and second, they have a converted dollar worth only 60 cents. If consideration is given to them it should be given immediately, and should be made effective at once.
Cost of Living

Mr. Speaker, I have only a minute or two at my disposal. It is hardly worth while my opening my main theme. I have been sitting here this evening listening to some of the remarks, and listening to the budget speech, and they made me think of a little nursery rhyme that I knew in my childhood. I remember that I had a book, I think it was called "Nonsense Rhymes." There was in it an ode addressed by humans to the world rolling in space, and it went something like this, although I will not take any responsibility for the correctness of my quotation. Yet I hardly think that any hon. member will mind very much if I am wrong in it. It went something like this: Roll on. thou ball, roll on!
What tho' I suffer numerous ills What tho' I swallow countless pills What tho' I cannot pay my bills?
Never you mind, ball, roll on.
When I think of that little nursery rhyme in relation to the demand for price control I think of this government as that ball which rolls on unheeding of the poor fellow who addressed it.
